walkthroughs.h2: What is in the air today
walkthroughs.body_html:
About 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen and around 1% argon plus small amounts of CO2 and water vapour.

These proportions have been roughly stable for the past 200 million years.

4.6 billion years ago: volcanoes released CO2, water vapour and nitrogen.

Water vapour condensed into oceans; CO2 dissolved into the oceans.

Plants evolved and removed CO2 via photosynthesis, releasing O2.

Short-wave radiation from the Sun reaches Earth and warms the surface.

Earth re-emits infrared radiation, which greenhouse gases absorb.

Main greenhouse gases: CO2, CH4 and water vapour.

mcqs.q: How does a catalyst speed up a reaction?
options: It provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy.
A catalyst gives extra kinetic energy to the reactant particles.
A catalyst lowers the activation energy of the original reaction pathway.
A catalyst increases the yield by being consumed in the forward reaction only.

mcqs.q: Why does increasing temperature increase the rate of reaction significantly?
options: A catalyst increases the yield by being consumed in the forward reaction only.
Mainly because a much larger fraction of collisions have energy at least equal to the activation energy; collision frequency increases only slightly.
Particles collide much more frequently at higher temperature, which is the main reason for the rate increase.
Higher temperature increases the concentration of the reactants.

mcqs.q: Does a catalyst affect the position of equilibrium?
options: Higher temperature increases the concentration of the reactants.
A catalyst increases the yield by being consumed in the forward reaction only.
No — it speeds up both the forward and reverse reactions equally, so equilibrium is reached faster but at the same position.
A catalyst shifts the equilibrium towards the products.

sequence.def: ~4.6 billion years ago: early atmosphere mostly CO2
Water vapour condenses; CO2 dissolves, forming sediments
~2.7 billion years ago: algae start releasing oxygen
CO2 trapped in sedimentary rocks and fossil fuels
About 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, plus small traces
Since ~1750 burning fossil fuels has pushed CO2 up
